analysis.one_liner: Bars health insurers from discriminating against dialysis patients and shifting their costs to Medicare.
analysis.headline: Introduced in March 2025 with bipartisan sponsorship and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, where no action has been taken.
analysis.plain_summary: People with kidney failure can keep their employer or private health plan as their main coverage for a period before Medicare takes over. The bill writes into law that private insurers may not single out dialysis patients for worse benefits, more limited networks, or disfavored coverage compared with other patients, and may not design coverage to push their costs onto Medicare. At the same time, it preserves insurers' ability to decide which dialysis providers are in their networks.
analysis.who_benefits: People with end-stage renal disease, roughly the several hundred thousand Americans on dialysis, gain protections against private plans that cut benefits, narrow networks, or otherwise make coverage worse for them specifically, and Medicare (taxpayers) is shielded from plans shifting dialysis costs onto it.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the Medicare Secondary Payer rules so private plans may not differentiate in benefits between people with end-stage renal disease and other enrollees, on any basis and in any manner [S3].
Plans may not apply any limitation on benefits, including limits on network composition, that would disparately affect people with kidney failure compared to other enrollees [S3].

The bill states a purpose of prohibiting health insurance plans from shifting primary responsibility for covering the cost of care needed by people with end-stage renal disease onto the Medicare program, which would otherwise raise federal costs [S3].

The bill responds to recent regulatory and litigation developments that weakened these anti-discrimination protections, aiming to restore the breadth of protections under the Medicare Secondary Payer Act [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Private health insurers and the employers and workers who pay premiums, because dialysis is extremely expensive care that insurers can no longer manage by disfavoring dialysis patients specifically or pushing their costs onto Medicare.

drawbacks.text: The bill acknowledges it does not change a plan's ability to limit which renal dialysis providers it includes in its network, so a patient cannot force their particular dialysis provider to be in-network, only get equal overall treatment [S3].

Because dialysis care is among the most expensive conditions to cover, preventing insurers from disfavoring dialysis patients or shifting those costs to Medicare likely raises premium costs spread across other plan enrollees and employers, a cost the bill does not offset.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the patients directly protected, the benefit is large: coverage they buy cannot be quietly made worse because they need dialysis. The cost is spread broadly through slightly higher premiums across everyone in private plans, which is a fair trade in principle but one the bill never tries to reduce. The carve-out preserving network design keeps the bill from going as far as dialysis advocates might want.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in March 2025 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which has taken no action on it since; Congress is still in session, so it could still move.

narrative.text: Sen. Bill Cassidy introduced the bill on March 27, 2025, joined at introduction by Sens. Booker, Cramer, and Heinrich [S3].
Seven senators, 2 Democrats and 5 Republicans, signed on as cosponsors, giving the bill support from both parties [S4].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance on the day it was introduced, and no further action appears in the record [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and the employers who fund group plans are better off so far, because the anti-discrimination rules have not been enacted and they retain current flexibility on dialysis coverage and costs. Dialysis patients keep their current coverage situation, which recent court and regulatory developments left unsettled.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill: 5 of 55 Senate Republicans and 2 of 45 Senate Democrats.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled any committee action on the bill since it was referred in March 2025; it sits with no markup or vote scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship is bipartisan: a Republican physician-senator leads, joined at introduction by a Democrat, and the cosponsor list splits 2 of 45 Democrats and 5 of 55 Republicans [S4].

industries.industry: Health insurers and employer health plans
industries.note: The bill removes their ability to design benefits or networks in ways that disfavor dialysis patients or push their costs onto Medicare, meaning they bear the full cost of a very expensive condition during the coordination period. Insurers challenged similar federal rules in court, which is part of why this bill exists [S3].

Keeping dialysis patients on commercial plans for longer means private plans, which pay dialysis providers far more than Medicare rates, remain their primary payer during the coordination period. The bill also preserves plans' ability to exclude particular dialysis providers from networks, a part the dialysis industry would prefer removed [S3].

analysis.trajectory: The bill has sat in the Senate Finance Committee since March 2025 with only seven cosponsors and no committee action. Most bills at this stage die in committee; the realistic paths forward are a Finance Committee markup or attachment to a larger health or Medicare package, neither of which appears imminent given the inaction to date.
